Figurative Meaning: “Return, return”—After it became known among the daughters of Jerusalem that she was ready to be borne and to return to her people and to her Beloved, they began to plead with her and entreat her not to leave them, saying: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return that we may look upon you,”“What will you see in the Shulammite?”the dance of the two camps—always surrounded by two encampments that stand guard over me? Thus I am as though a captive among you, constantly guarded on all sides by opposing forces.

She replies: “What will you gaze upon in the Shulammite?”the dance of the two camps—for I am surrounded by two opposing camps: one is the camp of God and the holy hosts, the side of the good inclination calling me to detach from all worldly desires and cleave to Torah, service, and holiness; and the other is the camp of the Satan and the armies of the evil inclination, the forces of the body, which seek that I fulfill bodily desires and material passions. How can I dwell peacefully among you between these two camps? “Woe to me from my Creator and woe to me from my inclination.”```

Figurative Meaning: “How beautiful are your footsteps”—The daughters of Jerusalem respond to the daughter of nobility: indeed, your steps are very beautiful—but only when you are wearing sandals. If you go out barefoot to your beloved shepherd, then your beauty is diminished. “The curves of your thighs are like ornaments,” like gold-worked jewelry, but only if they are adorned with ornaments made by an artisan. That is, your beauty is seen only when it is dressed in the proper garments and adornments; without them—when you go out to your beloved shepherd—you appear unadorned and lacking those external perfections.

Figurative Meaning: “How beautiful are your steps”—The daughters of the body respond to the soul of nobility, that is, the Divine soul: indeed, your steps are beautiful. This refers to the soul as the source of life for all three divisions of its faculties as described by the philosophers—the rational, the vital, and the vegetative soul. But when the soul is gathered to its people, all the bodily powers that depend on it are extinguished and cease to exist, and only the spirit returns to God who gave it. Therefore they address her and remind her that when she departs from them, all her functions in their various levels will cease. They arrange her actions from the lowest to the highest: first, motion, which is attributed to the feet, is indeed very beautiful, and thus they say, “How beautiful are your steps,” but this is only “in sandals,” meaning only while she is still clothed in the body, which is like a shoe (as explained earlier 5:3). But when she is called to “remove the sandal,” that is, when she sheds the material body from herself (as in “Remove your sandals from your feet,” meaning removal of materiality), then motion ceases entirely and the body remains like inert stone, unable to move from its place. Second, the vegetative soul’s powers, such as nourishment and generation, symbolized by the thighs, also cease at death. Thus “the curves of your thighs are like ornaments,”

Figurative Meaning: “Your navel” is likened to a round bowl that contains liquids within it, and it is accustomed to be filled with wine in abundance—see that it does not lack mixed wine, for in the house of the poor shepherd there will be no such lavish mixing of wine for you. “Your belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies,”

Figurative Meaning: “Your navel”—They speak to her concerning the faculty of nourishment, which is divided into eating and drinking, through which the body is sustained. They say: “Your navel is like a rounded bowl,” always filled with liquids and distributing its flow through channels to all the limbs of the body. See that this mixture does not cease, for at death the vessel will be broken at its spring, and this entire flow will be cut off, leaving that beautiful vessel—the bowl prepared to receive nourishment—utterly unused. Likewise “your belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies,”heap of wheat—for after death the wheat will no longer be given to the mill to be ground, and the grinders will cease with the fading of the sound of the millstone.

Figurative Meaning: “Your two breasts”—they are likened to two young gazelles in a place of beauty and delight, meaning in the inner chambers of the king where all treasures of desire are found, and not in the house of the poor shepherd.

Figurative Meaning: After having described the lower faculties—the instruments of the vegetative soul—he now turns to the higher faculties associated with the animal soul, whose dwelling is from the chest upward to the head, and notes the deficiency that will occur when she departs and is gathered to her people. “Your two breasts”—that is, the two powers of the soul, the irascible power and the appetitive power, which are “twin fawns,” meaning they are both offspring of the appetitive faculty (as explained earlier 4:5). They are likened to two young gazelles, but only insofar as they are “twins of a gazelle” within the material world, where the motivating faculty is aroused toward desire and beauty, and the irascible faculty toward jealousy and vengeance and the like. But if she is removed from this physical world, then the almond tree withers and the desires fail, and these powers cease from their activity.

Figurative Meaning: “Your neck” is likened to a tower of ivory, and your eyes to the pools in Heshbon, for they flow with freshness and vitality. All these excellencies, they say, are fitting to be found at the gate of the daughter of multitudes, in a city of perfect beauty, and not in a desolate wilderness. Likewise your nose, which is compared to the tower of Lebanon looking toward Damascus, should be situated toward a settled city and not toward a wasteland. Why then should all these perfect and beautiful faculties dwell alone in barren desert places, cut off from habitation and perfection?

Figurative Meaning: “Your neck” is a symbol of the rule of the intellect and the soul over the body and its appetitive powers, and it is compared to a tower of ivory, from which one fights enemies at the gate; so too from there the soul rules over the bodily faculties, subduing them under its authority (as explained earlier 4:4). Likewise “your eyes”—the eyes of intellect that see, contemplate, deliberate, and reflect on all matters of the body—are like pools where waters gather, for there all perceptions collected by the senses are assembled through the faculty of memory and preservation; they are pools of Heshbon, for they serve calculation, thought, and reckoning of all the ways and actions of the body, their benefits and deficiencies. Surely such faculties are fitting to stand at the gate of Bath-Rabbim, the gate of Jerusalem, which represents the body where the multitude of bodily powers gather and receive the governance and directives of the soul; but after death there is no longer any “weigher, scribe, or reckoner” in Sheol. Likewise “your nose” is compared to the tower of Lebanon, which represents the contemplative intellect—the face and form of the soul itself, since the essence of the soul is intellect. It is like a tower from which one surveys all the plantings of Lebanon and thus contemplates all the deeds established by God in His world and all His creations in the universe above and below. And this “nose” looks toward Damascus, meaning it contemplates the external, material world and all that is found from east to west; unlike the practical intellect which concerns itself only with Jerusalem, i.e., the body and its needs. Yet even this contemplative intellect, insofar as it engages the physical world (symbolized by Damascus, a land of the nations), ceases after death and no longer grasps material beings.

Figurative Meaning: “Your head upon you is like Carmel”—your head, which represents the highest intellectual faculty, is compared in its beauty and majesty to Mount Carmel, signifying exaltedness and splendor. And “the locks of your head are like purple”—the outward manifestations of that intellect appear in a noble and royal dignity. “The king is held captive in the tresses”—that is, even the supreme King, meaning the Divine influence, is bound and drawn, as it were, by the cords of love and attachment to the soul, unable to withdraw, as though constrained in bonds of love and delight.

Figurative Meaning: “Your head”—Here the “head that is upon you” refers to your essential self, the Divine and spiritual substance of the soul itself, which is the head over all your faculties. Thus it says “upon you,” meaning that as you truly are in your essence, this head is like Carmel, full of beauty and abundance, just as Carmel is filled with fruit and richness; so too you are filled with wisdom, knowledge of God, and holiness. Likewise “the hair of your head”—the locks and curls, which symbolize the emanations of intellectual lights that break forth from the soul’s essence and become revealed (as explained earlier in 4:1, 4:5, and 4:11, where hair represents the breaking forth of concealed light into manifestation)—are like purple, symbolizing the realm of the Divine throne, which is described by the mystics as “purple,” the domain of spiritual forces surrounding the Throne, lower than the realm of pure light and emanation from which holy souls originate. And “the king is held in the tresses”—that is, the body, which rules over the small city, is “bound” in the channels flowing from the soul, through which life, sensation, and understanding are drawn into the body; without them it cannot move at all and becomes like a stone. (And in the Midrash HaNe’elam, Vayikra 113b: Rabbi Pinchas said, the soul is taken from the Throne of Glory, which is the “head,” as it says “your head is like Carmel,” and “the hair of your head is like purple”—this is the soul—and “the king is held in the tresses” is the body, which is bound in the grave.)

Figurative Meaning: “How fair you are”—Here the quality of love is considered in an abstract sense. They say to the attribute of love itself: how beautiful and pleasant you are indeed—but only when you are joined with pleasures and delights. If love is connected to enjoyment, then it is considered beautiful and desirable, meaning that if you love the King in a way that brings you all delight and pleasure, then that love is good. But not so is the love directed toward a poor shepherd, in which there is no delight or sensory pleasure attached to it.

Figurative Meaning: “How fair you are”—“You are love itself,” they say, addressing the quality of love in abstraction: you are beautiful and exceedingly pleasant, but only when you are bound to pleasures and temporal delights. That is, if you love the body and live a life of transitory existence, then you will indeed have the pleasures and delights of time, and in that context your love is considered good. But not so in death, for then there are no pleasures or material delights to be found, and such love has no place there.

Figurative Meaning: “This”—Now King Solomon himself comes and speaks to her to prevent her from separating from him. He says to her: behold, this is your stature—you now stand upright with dignity and strength, so that you are likened to a tall palm tree, so lofty that no one can ascend to it. And your breasts are suspended from this height like clusters of fruit, hanging in fullness and beauty from your exalted stature.

Figurative Meaning: “This is your stature”—After portraying how all the faculties of the body and all its powers in their various divisions contend with the soul, each speaking to her individually and pleading that she not separate from them lest they perish through her departure, he now depicts how King Solomon himself—the heart, from which life flows and which is the pulse and vitality that persists until the final moment of death, gathering in itself the flow of blood and life—now separates from its beloved, the soul, and awakens for the last time with all its strength and powers to prevent her from departing from the body. (For it is known that at the final moment the heart exerts itself once more, as a lamp flares up before extinguishing.) He says to her: my soul, behold, “this is your stature,” meaning all the details previously described—from the feet up to the head—constitute the complete stature of the heavenly beloved soul. For the vegetative, animal, and rational faculties together form the full structure of the soul, from which these powers branch out (as explained by Maimonides in his Eight Chapters). And she is “like a palm tree,” which grows upward and whose heart is directed above; so too you are directed upward, and your desire is toward your Husband in heaven. And “your breasts are like clusters,” meaning that your powers have matured like grapes ready for harvest, to be placed in the winepress to produce wine; so too your time of harvest has arrived, to turn away from this world and receive the reward of your deeds in the world of recompense.

Figurative Meaning: Nevertheless, I said: “I will go up into the palm tree,”your breasts be like clusters of the vine—so that one who holds them may drink the wine of the grape and become refreshed with its strength—and that the fragrance of your breath be like apples, giving forth a pleasant and delightful aroma.

Figurative Meaning: Nevertheless, “I said, I will go up into the palm tree,”hold on to its branches, a metaphor for the body’s final struggle to retain the soul so that it does not separate. “Let your breasts be like clusters of the vine,”“the fragrance of your breath like apples,”

Figurative Meaning: “And your palate is like the best wine”—up to here are the words of King Solomon. The beloved replies: “It goes down to my Beloved.” That is, the sweetness of my palate is not for you, but belongs to my Beloved the Shepherd; therefore do not ascend further to my stature, for I am now going to my Beloved and I belong to Him. “I am my Beloved’s,”“His desire is toward me,”

Figurative Meaning: “And your palate”—that is, your inner speech of wisdom (as explained earlier on “your mouth is sweetness”), shall be like the best wine, which symbolizes the spirit of holiness, the “good wine” mentioned throughout this book, meaning that the soul consents that if she continues to live she will devote herself only to Torah, wisdom, commandments, holiness, and knowledge of God. She replies: “I am going to my Beloved,”“I am going to the straightnesses,”“causing the lips of sleepers to speak,”

Figurative Meaning: “I am my Beloved’s and His desire is toward me,” for the soul departs in the “kiss” of death and longing, in a union of desire between the part and the whole and the whole and the part, and she cleaves to her source out of the greatness of her love. (And see Aderet Ha’azinu, p. 288, where Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is recorded as having uttered this verse at the moment of his passing.)
Figurative Meaning: “Come, my beloved”—The beloved soul turns her face toward her Beloved and says: “Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field,”“Let us lodge in the villages,”

Figurative Meaning: “Come, my beloved”—Now that the soul has departed from the body, she turns her face toward her supreme Beloved, who stands over her to gather her unto Himself, and says: “Come, my beloved, let us go out from here,”“Let us go out into the field,”“Let us lodge in the villages,”“let us lodge in the villages,”chibbut hakever (the “purgation of the grave”).
Figurative Meaning: “Let us rise early in the morning to the vineyards,”“Let us see whether the vine has blossomed and the pomegranates have budded,”“there I will give you my love,”

Figurative Meaning: “Let us rise early” in the morning to the vineyards—here the “vineyards” symbolize, as already explained, the ultimate purpose of all actions and deeds, meaning we will examine what fruit was produced from all our labor and activity in the corporeal world. “Let us see whether the vine has blossomed,”“the tender grape has opened,”“the pomegranates have budded,”“there I will give you my love,”

Figurative Meaning: “The mandrakes give forth fragrance”—the beloved soul says: behold, even the mandrakes that are gathered for their pleasant scent, nevertheless their fragrance is not reserved for their owners alone, for they are ownerless in the field and have already given their scent to all who pass by. And likewise all kinds of delights are “at our gates,” meaning all pleasures and delights that serve bodily enjoyment are open and accessible to everyone, and though they may appear new, they are in truth like old things, since one becomes fully satiated with them and they lose their importance. But “my beloved and my love I have stored up for you,”

And <b>“at our gates are all precious fruits,”</b meaning the fruits of action are outside the inner sanctum; they remain at the threshold and do not enter the inner chambers of the heart, for deeds performed without love of God are like bodies without a soul—husks without inner content—standing at the entrance but not entering within. And <b>“new as well as old,”</b meaning even important commandments become “old” when performed only out of habit, as learned behavior without inner devotion, like the commandments of men learned by rote. But <b>“my beloved I have stored up for you,”</b meaning the love of God—the service performed מתוך אהבה—is what is reserved solely for Him, hidden and dedicated entirely to God alone, and is wholly sanctified.```

Figurative Meaning: “O that you were like a brother to me”—the beloved soul laments that she had to leave the house of her mother and her family, meaning her original spiritual source and familiar attachments, and wander with her Beloved through fields and wilderness. She says: would that You were to me like a brother who nursed at my mother’s breasts, so that even if I would kiss You in public, I would not be despised or regarded with shame, meaning that our intimate spiritual union would be openly recognized and not hidden or constrained by the limitations of the corporeal world.

She now longs for the level of Moses and Elijah, who were not hindered by the body and its inclinations from constant cleaving to the spiritual realm, and who had the ability to cast off their “defiled garments” at will and separate from the body into prophecy and Divine attachment, even dwelling as it were both above and within, in a state of constant ascent and return, clothed in “garments of light” and drawing Divine glory into their inner chamber so that it would dwell within them. Thus she says: <b>“O that You were like a brother to me,”</b meaning that God would be bound to the soul as a brother (for the soul is called the sister of the King from its higher root), and <b>“like one who nursed at my mother’s breasts,”</b meaning that if the soul is the body (as explained earlier), then even bodily actions would be accepted and nourished as service. And this would be in two ways: <b>“I would find You outside and kiss You,”</b meaning I would be able to go out beyond the limits of the body and find God there, cleaving to Him and receiving His Divine embrace, and <b>“they would not despise me,”</b meaning the faculties of the body, the “daughters of Jerusalem,” would not obstruct or mock her, but would allow her to separate and unite with her Beloved at all times.```

Figurative Meaning: And I would also be able to guide You and bring You into the house of my mother, meaning into the innermost source from which I was drawn. And there “you would teach me,”“I would give You to drink of spiced wine,”

Figurative Meaning: (Secondly) “I would lead You and bring You to the house of my mother,” meaning into my corporeal existence, and there “You would teach me” Your Torah and commandments, that is, the Divine service I would perform while still clothed in flesh and body. And “I would give You to drink of spiced wine,”“of the juice of my pomegranates,”

Figurative Meaning: “And that His left hand would be under my head openly”—meaning that even in the revealed and manifest state, the Divine support and sustaining Providence would be extended to the soul in a clear and public way, so that her dependence upon Him and her attachment to Him would not be hidden or concealed, but would be openly recognized in her existence within the world of action and embodiment.

Figurative Meaning: And that “His left hand would be under my head”—as I have already explained earlier (2:6), the “left hand” symbolizes intellectual apprehension and rational understanding, while the “right hand” symbolizes prophetic apprehension, which is purer and free of any admixture. Thus the meaning is that the pure and elevated apprehension of Divine inspiration (Ruach HaKodesh) would become the primary and dominant form of perception, surpassing the lower mode of intellectual understanding that arises through philosophical inquiry and analytical reasoning, as explained above.

Figurative Meaning: “I adjure you”—she concludes her words addressing the daughters of Jerusalem, whom she has often adjured by the hosts or by the gazelles. But now she says that she is no longer afraid of them, for “what can you awaken or stir up?”—you are no longer able to disturb or suppress this love in any way, for it has reached a state in which it cannot be interrupted or overcome by any external influence.

Figurative Meaning: “I adjure you”—however, she returns again to her words and says: you, daughters of Jerusalem, which are the powers of the body, “have I not adjured you” often “by the gazelles or by the hinds of the field,”“what can you awaken or stir up love?”

Figurative Meaning: “Who is this”—the poet asks: who is this that has moved away from the settled city into the wilderness and yet clings affectionately to her beloved? And the Beloved answers: “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” meaning at the very place where I first found you, I found you asleep under the apple tree, and there I awakened you; and there again, under the apple tree, your mother travailed with you and gave birth to you. And there too your mother herself was born. Thus it is fitting that you dwell in the wilderness rather than in the city, for both you and your ancestors were formed and found there, and you are accustomed to that place from your origin.
The answer: “Under the apple tree I awakened you,”“There your mother was in labor with you,”“there she who bore you was in labor with you,”```

Figurative Meaning: “Set me as a seal upon your heart”—the beloved soul asks of her Beloved that He place her like a permanent seal upon His heart and upon His arm, meaning that she should be constantly remembered and guarded in both His inner love and His outward governance, so that she may be protected from the wrath of the King, for her love is strong as death, since she has given her life for His love. Yet the jealousy of the King is severe like Sheol because she has left Him, and therefore only the flames of her love can overcome even that severity, for they are flames of fire, a flame of God, stronger than the fire of judgment itself.

Figurative Meaning: “Set me as a seal”—the soul asks of her heavenly Beloved that He place her as a seal upon His heart and upon His arm, meaning that she be united with Him in both intention and action, in love and in manifestation, so that she may be constantly bound to His will and His governance. For “love is strong as death,”the jealousy of the evil inclination is as strong as Sheol, seeking to draw her away from Divine service and cast her into the depths of destruction, nevertheless the flames of the love of God that burn within her are flames of fire, a flame of Hashem, which overcome and consume the forces of temptation and the seductions of the evil inclination. Therefore, since she has always struggled with it and prevailed, she is worthy to be placed as a seal upon His heart and His arm, receiving her reward both in Divine will and in revealed action.

Figurative Meaning: “Many waters”—the poet observes the immense power of love and its fiery flames, declaring that “many waters cannot quench it” nor can floods extinguish it, meaning that all of Solomon’s attempts and strategies to turn the beloved soul away from her Beloved were completely ineffective. For the fire of love cannot be extinguished by abundant waters, nor can rivers that normally sweep away all things in their path overcome it; thus neither persuasion nor force, neither kindness nor coercion, could succeed. Therefore, “if a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly despised,”

Figurative Meaning: The beloved soul cleaves to her Beloved—that is, the soul has reached a state of complete attachment and unity with her Divine source, where no external force, power, or obstruction can separate her from Him, and she remains bound in enduring love and unbreakable devotion.
And with this the fifth song is completed.

Figurative Meaning: “Many waters”—the poet declares: “Many waters cannot quench love,”“Nor can rivers overwhelm it,”“if a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly despised,”

Figurative Meaning: The beloved soul of Solomon cleaves to the eternal life, the God of the spirits of all flesh—meaning the perfected soul has now reached complete attachment to her Divine source, the “Life of all lives,” from whom all spirits are drawn, and she remains bound to Him in everlasting unity without separation.
And with this the fifth song is completed.

Figurative Meaning: The Song of Songs: In this song it is told that the beloved soul pleads on behalf of her younger sister, lest the King desire her as well, and it further describes the response of the Beloved and of her sister.

Figurative Meaning: The sister of the beloved says: we have a younger sister who has not yet developed her “breasts,” meaning she has not yet reached maturity of faculties and readiness for full spiritual union. What shall we do for her on the day she will be spoken for, when she is to be joined to the King, lest King Solomon desire to take her for himself?

Figurative Meaning: The Song of Songs of a Thousand: This song describes how the soul pours out her plea before God on behalf of her younger sister, which is the potential, undeveloped spirit, that it should not be taken by the “king,” meaning that it should not become overly attached to the body and perish with it. It also includes the response of the Holy One, blessed be He, and the response of the spirit itself regarding this matter.

Yet through proper deeds, Torah, and Divine service, a kind of “alchemical” refinement is performed upon it, until it becomes purified and acquires an enduring, incorporeal nature, so that it may remain alive after the death of the body. And as the sages of truth have explained at length, the spirit remains in the lower Garden of Eden, while the higher Divine soul ascends above and at times “clothes itself” within it when it descends. Therefore the higher soul says: we have a little sister, meaning the spirit, but <b>“she has no breasts,”</b meaning she does not give forth influence, since she is an acquired intellect rather than an emanated intellect; she only receives rather than bestows. And <b>“what shall we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?”</b meaning: if she is taken into the “house of the king,” that is, into the body and physical existence of Solomon, will she be destroyed together with it in the grave, or how will she be preserved so as to remain in eternal life?```

Figurative Meaning: “The Beloved answers”—If she is a wall, meaning if the lower soul remains closed and firm like a wall, not yielding itself to the attraction of the body, then we will build upon her a silver tower, meaning she will be protected and elevated by a strong spiritual structure of longing and refinement (for “silver” alludes to yearning and desire), and she will be given a partner who will direct her longing toward God, through whom she will be drawn out from the domain of Solomon, that is, the body. But if she is a door, meaning if she is open and inclined toward the desires of Solomon, then we will enclose her with a cedar plank, meaning she will be left to him and bound within the structure of the physical world, since cedar represents durability in the material order and thus indicates her remaining within corporeal limitation.
Figurative Meaning: “If”—the Holy One, blessed be He, answers: “If she is a wall,”“we will build upon her a tower of silver,”“if she is a door,”“we will enclose her with a cedar board,”
Figurative Meaning: The sister replies: “I am a wall,”“my breasts are like towers,”“I was in his eyes as one who finds peace,”
Figurative Meaning: “I”—the spirit replies: “I was a wall,”“my breasts,”“were like towers,”“I was in his eyes as one who finds peace,”
Figurative Meaning: “And the proof of this is: Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon,”“the vineyard was so large that its keepers each brought a thousand silver pieces for its fruit,”

And <b>“he gave the vineyard to keepers,”</b meaning all the forces of the body, called the “people of Jerusalem,” were appointed as its keepers: the intellectual powers tended the vines of contemplation and knowledge, while the life-forces tended the clusters of commandments and deeds. And <b>“each man brought a thousand silver pieces for its fruit,”</b meaning that from all these activities there emerged abundant reward and valuable, desirable attainments of great worth.```

Figurative Meaning: And this is my vineyard, which stands before me, for Solomon gave me this vineyard as a gift because I was in his eyes as one who finds peace. But she then retracts her words and says: I do not wish to retain this vineyard for myself; rather, the thousand pieces of silver that were brought as the reward of the vineyard shall be yours, Solomon, and I will also return the two hundred that belong to the keepers of its fruit, for I do not seek to derive benefit from this vineyard at all.

But she then concludes that Solomon himself—the body and its faculties that labored in this vineyard through Torah and service—will not be deprived of his reward, for they will rest in the grave in sleep and will arise at the appointed time at the end of days (as explained in Zohar Va’era 28b). Therefore she says: <b>“The thousand are for you, Solomon,”</b meaning the reward of the vineyard’s fruits—commandments and good deeds—also belongs to the body and the lower soul, for they too have their recompense. And <b>“the two hundred for those who keep its fruit,”</b meaning, as stated in Midrash Ne’elam (Chayei Sarah 124), every righteous person engaged in Torah is granted two hundred worlds and treasures as reward for the Torah.```

Figurative Meaning: “O you who dwell in the gardens”—the Beloved speaks to the younger sister, meaning the soul that has not yet withdrawn into the wilderness like her elder sister, but remains within the “gardens,” that is, within the closer and more settled realms adjacent to the body and the city. And because she is still near the “city,” there are companions who listen to her words. Yet the Beloved says that He cannot fully unite with her in close intimacy; rather, only “let Me hear your voice,”

Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, says to the spirit: <b>“You who dwell in the gardens,”</b meaning you who remain in the garden of the lower Eden and do not continuously ascend to the higher world, <b>“there are companions who listen,”</b meaning the spirit is connected to the soul beneath it, and the soul is connected to the body that remains in the grave; since it is close to them, the spirit cannot always attach itself to the Beloved in full union. Therefore it is only <b>“let Me hear your voice,”</b meaning only at designated times and intervals does your spiritual ascent reach Me.```
Figurative Meaning: And she too becomes fearful of the “watchers,” meaning the opposing forces that hinder spiritual ascent, and she says: “Flee, my beloved,”“be like a gazelle or a young stag,”
Figurative Meaning: And likewise the spirit says to God: “Flee, my beloved,”“be like a gazelle or a young stag,”
